Clinical Development Success Rates and Contributing Factors

Automated Pipeline Analysis
Generated April 2026

Executive Summary

Key Takeaways
  • The overall likelihood of approval (LOA) from Phase 1 for all developmental candidates was 28.8% (n=24,721).
  • Phase II remains the largest hurdle in clinical development, with only 58.4% of candidates achieving this transition (n=7,844).
  • Of the major disease areas, Ophthalmology had the highest LOA from Phase 1 (43.9%, n=663), representing a 3.2-fold increase over Oncology (13.6%).
  • The LOA from Phase 1 for non-oncology indications (33.5%) was nearly 2-fold higher than oncology (13.6%).
  • Among drug modalities, peptide achieved the highest LOA from Phase 1 at 31.2%.
  • On average, it takes 17.6 years for a Phase 1 asset to progress to regulatory approval.
  • 2,519 unique sponsors contributed, with 1,255 (50%) having a single candidate.

Introduction

This study aimed to measure clinical drug development success rates, contributing factors to those outcomes, and timelines of clinical trials. With the goal of providing current benchmarking metrics for drug development, this study covers individual drug program phase transitions over 1931–2022.

A total of 24,721 clinical and regulatory phase transitions were recorded and analyzed from 11,099 development programs across 2,519 sponsors. Phase transitions occur when a drug candidate advances into the next phase of development or is suspended by the sponsor. By calculating the number of programs progressing to the next phase vs the total number progressing and suspended, we assessed the success rate at each of the four phases of development: Phase I, II, III, and regulatory filing.

Having phase-by-phase data in hand, we then compared groups of diseases, drug modalities, and other attributes to generate a comprehensive analysis of drug development success.

Part 1. Phase Transition Success and Likelihood of Approval

Phase Transition Success Rates

Success rates for individual phases of the drug development process were determined by dividing the number that successfully advanced to the next phase by the total number advanced and suspended. This ‘advanced and suspended’ number is often referred to as ‘n’ in this report and should be taken into account when drawing conclusions from the success rate results.

The Phase 1 transition success rate was 86.4% (n=9,080). As this phase is typically conducted for safety testing and is not dependent on efficacy for candidates to advance, it is common for this phase to have a higher success rate among the clinical phases.

The Phase 2 transition success rate (58.4%, n=7,844) was substantially lower than Phase 1, and the lowest of the four phases studied. As this is generally the first stage where proof-of-concept is deliberately tested in human subjects, Phase 2 consistently has the lowest success rate of all phases. This is also the point in development where industry must decide whether to pursue large, expensive Phase 3 studies, or to terminate development.

The second-highest phase transition success rate was found in Phase 3 (70.3%, n=4,579). This is significant as most company-sponsored Phase 3 trials are the longest and most expensive trials to conduct.

The probability of approval after submitting an NDA or BLA, taking into account resubmissions, was 81.3% (n=3,218).

Phase-Transition Heatmaps

Major disease areas were segmented according to therapeutic convention, yielding 14 major groupings. The ordering of disease areas below is consistent with the overall likelihood of approval from Phase 1, which is analyzed later in the LOA section.

Success rates by disease area for Phase 1 ranged from 73.9% to 95.7%, with the average for all indications at 86.4%. Endocrine and the other leading disease areas were well above the average rate. With the exception of these top performers, the remainder were all within a reasonable distance from the mean.

In every disease area, Phase 2 had the lowest transition success rate of the four phases. Phase 2 success rates ranged from a high of 78.4% (Ophthalmology, n=190) to a low of 36.8% (Oncology, n=1,579). This 42 percentage-point range of disparity between major disease areas at the Phase 2 transition is the major contributor to the observed divergences in overall likelihood of approval (LOA), as discussed in the next section.

With only Ophthalmology (78.4%), Cardiovascular (75.6%), Metabolic (71.4%), Infectious disease (68.8%), Others (67.1%), Endocrine (62.5%), Psychiatry (62.5%), Respiratory (62.3%), Neurology (60.8%), Autoimmune (59.1%) achieving Phase 2 success rates above the overall average of 58.4%, these disease areas are also the leaders when calculating the overall LOA from Phase 1.

The lowest-performing disease groups were Oncology (36.8%).

For Phase 3 transition success rates, Oncology had the lowest rate at 62.8% (n=581). 7 disease group(s) ranked below the average Phase 3 transition success rate of 70.3%.

NDA/BLA transition success rates (approval rates) for the major disease areas ranged from 74.8% (Infectious disease) to 86.7% (Cardiovascular). This distribution had the tightest range among the four phases analyzed in this report.

Interactive Bubble Heatmaps

Likelihood of Approval

One of the key measures of success used in this report is the LOA from Phase 1. The LOA success rate is simply a multiplication of success rates from all four phases, a compounded probability calculation. For example, if each phase had a 50% chance of success, then the LOA from Phase 1 would be 0.5 × 0.5 × 0.5 × 0.5 = 6.25%.

Multiplying the individual phase probabilities across all disease areas, the compounded probability of progressing from Phase 1 to FDA approval reveals that only 28.8% of drug development programs (n=24,721) successfully make it to market.

As can be seen in the figure below, there is a wide range of LOAs from Phase 1. At the high end, Ophthalmology towers over the other disease groups at 43.9% (n=663). Ophthalmology therapies had an LOA from Phase 1 3 times higher than Oncology, which had the lowest LOA at 13.6% (n=4,662).

After Ophthalmology, 9 other disease area(s) were above the overall average of 28.8%: Cardiovascular, Metabolic, Others, Autoimmune, Endocrine, Psychiatry, Respiratory, Infectious disease, Neurology.

Falling under the overall LOA of 28.8% were Oncology. The fact that some of these disease categories carry large n values while also having low LOA values indicates that they are significant contributors in bringing down the overall LOA.

Looking deeper into drug modality, peptide development has seen the most success among the modalities studied. At 31.2% (n=1,156), the Phase 1 LOA for peptide therapies is slightly higher than the 28.8% average across all diseases.

Other modalities with above-average LOAs include small_molecule (30.3%), fusion_protein (29.1%).

At the lower end, gene_therapy had a Phase 1 LOA of 0.0% (n=33).

As an approximate rule, the increasing chemical and biological complexity of the therapeutic being tested is associated with higher rates of phase success. Advanced biologic therapies possess the intrinsic benefit of being precise tools for manipulating human biology and are reserved for indications where there is a clear pathophysiology. Additionally, they are more likely to benefit indirectly by association with other factors that are highly predictive of success, including regulatory designation and biomarker-enriched patient populations.

Oncology vs Non-Oncology

Oncology drug development program transitions accounted for 19% of the 24,721 total transitions. With an LOA from Phase 1 of 13.6% (n=4,662), Oncology had an outsized effect on the overall success rate. To further understand this contribution, we compared phase transition success rates and LOA for non-oncology development programs against oncology programs.

The LOA from Phase 1 across non-oncology indications, 33.5% (n=20,059), was nearly 2-fold higher than oncology alone at 13.6% (n=4,662). Comparing individual phase transition success rates, Oncology consistently had one of the lowest success rates for every developmental clinical transition.

In particular, there were relative differentials between Oncology and non-oncology groupings: Phase 1→Phase 2: 73.9% vs 90.2%; Phase 2→Phase 3: 36.8% vs 63.8%; Phase 3→Approval: 62.8% vs 71.4%.

Part 2. Drug Development Timelines

Drug Development Timelines

In addition to determining whether drugs are advanced or suspended at the end of a phase transition, the data can also be analyzed to yield time spent at each clinical stage, and overall drug development timelines. These are valuable metrics as there are considerable opportunity costs associated with investing in an R&D process that may take up to a decade.

Based on successful phase transitions, it took an average of 17.6 years for a drug to successfully progress from Phase 1 development to regulatory approval. This includes 5.6 years at Phase 1, 6.4 years at Phase 2, 5.7 years at Phase 3.

Phase duration can vary greatly according to numerous factors, such as disease area and indication, best practices of clinical trial design, and patient availability.

Disease areas with above-average LOAs tend to be associated with shorter development timelines. 12 of the disease areas fall beneath the 17.6-year average development duration. Conversely, the remaining disease areas with below-average LOAs either have durations close to the average or notably exceed it.

Metabolic had the shortest overall development duration at 8.2 years, while Hematology had the longest at 24.6 years.

Part 3. Temporal and Structural Analysis

LOA by Time Period

To examine temporal trends, candidates were partitioned into 2 time periods based on their earliest trial start date (517 candidates excluded due to missing dates).

Weighted average LOA from Phase 1 across periods: 1931–2004: 32.6%; 2005–2022: 26.5%.

Disease areas showing improvement: Ophthalmology (37.3% → 48.5%).

Disease areas showing decline: Others (41.6% → 35.1%); Gastroenterology (27.1% → 22.2%); Autoimmune (40.7% → 33.0%).

Drug Modality Composition Over Time

The composition of drug modalities in clinical development was tracked across 46 years (1931–2022).

Sponsor Concentration

A total of 2,519 unique sponsors were identified across all development programs. 1,255 sponsors (50%) contributed just a single candidate, while the top 10 sponsors accounted for 26% of all candidates.

The leading sponsors by candidate count were: National Cancer Institute (NCI) (814), National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases (NIAID) (390), GlaxoSmithKline (295).

Discussion

Discussion

The Phase 2 transition is clearly the main translational and limiting step from bench to bedside, as proof-of-concept is only established in 58.4% of drug programs at this stage. Phase 2 also sees the greatest distribution between major disease areas. Within these disease areas, it is the performance of novel drug classes that has the most significant negative contribution to low overall LOA success rates.

The average timeline from Phase 1 to approval was 17.6 years. This lengthy timeframe is a significant risk to investors and entrepreneurs, and speaks to the current complexities of clinical drug development. This risk is compounded by the correlation of longer timelines in certain disease areas with greater pipeline attrition rates. Disease areas with above-average LOAs tend to have the shortest development timelines, while those with below-average LOAs often carry longer development durations.

As an approximate rule, the increasing chemical complexity of the therapeutic being tested is associated with higher rates of phase success. However, it will be interesting to see whether leading modalities can sustain high LOAs as additional programs enter the clinic and attempt to extend the technology into new, unproven treatment settings. Success rates can eventually decline over time as sample sizes increase and the competitive landscape intensifies.
